_metadata.description: Persons in the 15th-century medical-alchemical-pharmaceutical network relevant to Voynich provenance
_metadata.region: Northern Italy, Southern Germany, Austria (Vienna), Switzerland, Alsace

persons.name: Taddeo Alderotti
persons.significance: Pioneered fractional distillation of alcohol; first water-cooled coil condenser; ~90% ethanol purity

persons.name: Arnald of Villanova
persons.significance: Introduced distilled alcohol to Western medicine; massive pseudo-Arnaldian corpus circulated in 15th C

persons.name: Peter of Abano
persons.significance: Foundational figure for Padua medical-philosophical tradition; synthesized Greek, Arabic, Jewish, Latin traditions; suspected of alchemy

persons.name: William of Saliceto
persons.significance: Premier surgeon of Bologna; promoted surgical knife over cauterization; teacher of Lanfranchi

persons.name: Lanfranchi of Milan
persons.significance: Chirurgia Magna (1296); 70+ editions; argued medicine and surgery inseparable; autobiographical epilogue

persons.name: Ortolf von Baierland
persons.significance: Arzneibuch (~1300): foundational German-language medical textbook; ~70 complete MSS + 130 excerpts; peak popularity 15th C

persons.name: John of Rupescissa
persons.significance: De consideratione quintae essentiae (~1351): foundational text linking distillation to universal medicine; 10 German MSS by 15th C; Brunschwig's primary theoretical source
persons.voynich_relevance: HIGH - our existing Rupescissa connection (F-BRU series); quintessence = distillation theory behind Voynich procedures

persons.name: Guy de Chauliac
persons.significance: Chirurgia Magna (1363): hugely influential; translated into all European vernaculars EXCEPT German (notable absence)

persons.name: Konrad von Megenberg
persons.significance: Buch der Natur (~1350): first natural history in German; 100+ surviving MSS; first printed 1475

persons.name: Giovanni de Dondi
persons.significance: Padua professor of medicine and astronomy; manuscripts ended up in Vienna (ONB Lat. 5208) — direct Padua-Vienna MS transmission

persons.name: Galeazzo di Santa Sofia
persons.significance: Member of Padua's most prominent medical dynasty (father Giovanni, uncle Marsilio, brother Bartolomeo). Taught at University of Vienna 1394/95-1405; personal physician to Duke Albrecht IV of Austria. Performed first public anatomical dissection north of the Alps in Vienna in 1404. Returned to Padua in 1406, taught theoretical medicine until death from plague in 1427. Served as DEGREE PROMOTER for Giovanni Fontana (arts 1418, medicine 1421) — a documented one-hop connection between Vienna and a Padua cipher-maker during the Voynich radiocarbon window.
persons.voynich_relevance: VERY HIGH - bridges Fontana's Padua cipher workshop to the Vienna court; at Vienna 1394-1405 (exact radiocarbon start); personal physician to the Austrian Duke; promoted the only known Padua physician who created an invented cipher alphabet

persons.name: Michele Savonarola
persons.significance: First treatise entirely dedicated to distilled spirits (Libreto de Aqua Ardente, 1444-1450); Padua professor of practical medicine; court physician to House of Este; grandfather of Girolamo Savonarola

persons.name: Nicolo Roccabonella
persons.significance: Liber de simplicibus (c.1445): 458 chapters, illustrated by Andrea Amadio; handwritten for his son in medical school; Padua medical milieu

persons.name: Michael Puff von Schrick
persons.significance: 11-time Dean of Vienna medical faculty (1435-1470); personal physician to Archduke Albrecht II; Buchlein von den ausgebrannten Wassern (~1455, printed 1477); 31 incunabula editions; specialist in medicine, anatomy, and chemistry; first female dissection in Vienna (1452); Brunschwig's acknowledged main source
persons.voynich_relevance: HIGH - Vienna medical faculty during Voynich period; distillation specialist; institutional power

persons.name: Johannes Hartlieb
persons.patron: Duke Albrecht III, then Duke Sigmund of Bavaria-Munich
persons.significance: Krauterbuch (c.1440/1462): 160 plants; Buch aller verbotenen Kunst (1456): treatise on forbidden arts and magic; oldest known description of witches' flying ointment; BRIDGES medicine and occult knowledge
persons.voynich_relevance: MEDIUM - Munich court physician combining herbal medicine with occult/secret knowledge traditions

persons.name: Johannes de Ketham
persons.significance: Professor of medicine at Vienna, CONTEMPORARY of Puff von Schrick; associated with Fasciculus medicinae (1491, Venice): first printed medical book with anatomical illustrations; Vienna-Venice publishing axis
persons.voynich_relevance: MEDIUM - direct colleague of Puff at Vienna; shows Vienna-Venice connections

persons.name: Gabriel von Lebenstein
persons.significance: Von den gebrannten Wassern: one of earliest German-language distilled waters treatises; precursor to Puff

persons.name: Hieronymus Brunschwig
persons.significance: Liber de arte distillandi (1500, 1512): first printed distillation manual; Chirurgia (1497); explicitly REVEALED previously hidden knowledge ('geoffenbart'); drew heavily on Rupescissa (1/3 of Large Book); used Puff as main source; claimed 3000 books read; no university education confirmed
persons.voynich_relevance: HIGH - acknowledged the existence of a prior secrecy tradition; his work is the 'open' successor to whatever was encoded before

persons.name: Johann Gruninger
persons.significance: Printed Brunschwig's Chirurgia (1497), Small Book (1500), Large Book (1512); also printed Salicetus's Antidotarius animae (1489); up to 80 books/year; key node in Strasbourg printing network

persons.name: Nicolaus Salicetus
persons.significance: Doctor of arts AND medicine from Paris; Cistercian abbot in Strasbourg diocese; Antidotarius animae printed by Gruninger (1489); potential bridge between academic and monastic knowledge traditions
persons.voynich_relevance: MEDIUM - same printer as Brunschwig; dual medical-monastic credentials; under-researched

persons.name: Niklas Jankowitz
persons.significance: Leader of alchemist circle that created the Alchymey Teuczsch (Cpg 597, 1426); invented three cipher alphabets; directed gold multiplication experiments (1423); stated 'We ourselves created this new alphabet so that one would not recognize it as an alphabet'; likely successor to Jewish alchemist Salman Teublein; probably served the Landgraves of Leuchtenberg
persons.voynich_relevance: VERY HIGH - cipher manuscript from same region/period as Voynich

persons.name: Michael von Prapach
persons.significance: Collaborator on the Alchymey Teuczsch; authored Verworfene Tage (Rejected/Unlucky Days, fols. 47v-48r) — astrological calendar specifying which days and times were suitable for alchemical experiments; references 'the masters' as authorities

persons.name: Michael Wulfing
persons.significance: Collaborator on the Alchymey Teuczsch; authored magical and medical texts including Beschworung gegen Fieber (incantation against fever, fol. 48r) and a love spell requiring specific ritual timing; bridges alchemical and magical traditions

persons.name: Giovanni Fontana
alt_names: Giovanni Jacopo Antonio de la Fontana
persons.significance: Used an entirely invented cipher alphabet — 23 symbols constructed exclusively from circles and straight lines — in at least 2 works: Bellicorum instrumentorum liber (c.1420, BSB Cod.icon. 242) and Secretum de thesauro experimentorum (c.1430, BnF). Cipher is simple monoalphabetic substitution of Latin, fully deciphered by Battisti & Saccaro (1984). Design is systematic: vowels share a circle base with directional tickmarks (cardinal mnemonic); consonants grouped by morphological similarity (mirror groups B/D/P/Q, stroke-count groups H/K/M/N). Degree promoters at Padua included GALEAZZO DI SANTA SOFIA (P011), who had spent 1394-1405 at Vienna — a documented one-hop connection to the Austrian court. Also studied under Prosdocimo de Beldomandi (mathematician/astronomer) and Paolo Nicoletti da Udine (Paul of Venice, major logician). Later career: municipal physician at Udine.
persons.voynich_relevance: VERY HIGH - Padua physician using invented cipher alphabet at exact Voynich radiocarbon date (1404-1438); degree promoter Galeazzo bridges directly to Vienna; cipher design shows systematic glyph construction (circles + lines) with vowel/consonant family distinction — closest known design philosophy to Voynich script

persons.name: Niccolo Falcucci
persons.significance: Sermones medicinales (~1400): medical encyclopedia; 'obligatory reference' for medical students; printed Pavia 1481-84, Venice 1491

persons.name: Georg Peuerbach
persons.significance: Court astrologer; teacher of Regiomontanus; key Vienna intellectual

persons.name: Regiomontanus
persons.significance: Student of Peuerbach at Vienna; lectured at Padua 1464; demonstrates Vienna-Padua academic traffic

persons.name: Konrad Celtis
persons.significance: Founded humanist network spanning Italy and Vienna; College of Poets and Mathematicians at Vienna (1501); demonstrates the Italy-Vienna intellectual circuit

persons.name: Heinrich von Pfalzpaint
persons.significance: Wundarznei (1460): battlefield surgery; first German-language rhinoplasty description; 11 MSS

persons.name: Johann Wonnecke von Kaub
persons.significance: Gart der Gesundheit (1485): first printed illustrated German herbal; 435 chapters, 379 woodcuts; expanded into Hortus sanitatis (1491)

persons.name: Philipp Ulstad
persons.significance: Coelum philosophorum (1525): major quintessence work; synthesized Rupescissa, pseudo-Arnald, pseudo-Lull, Brunschwig; 20+ editions

persons.name: Hans von Gersdorff
persons.significance: Feldbuch der Wundarzney (1517): military surgery; 40 years battlefield experience; same city as Brunschwig, published by Schott (another major Strasbourg printer)

persons.name: Hartmann Schedel
persons.significance: Nuremberg Chronicle (1493); personal library had 370 MSS + 670 printed books by 1498 — documents the MS-to-print overlap period; medical doctorate from Padua

persons.name: Johannes Tichtel
persons.significance: Studied medicine at Vienna from 1463; Doctor of Medicine 1476; Dean ten times (1482-1498); diary (1477-1495) is major cultural-historical document; overlapped with tail end of Puff's career

persons.name: Benedikt Planckh
persons.significance: Transcribed and expanded Puff von Schrick's work; cited additional sources: Peter of Ulm, Karg von Innsbruck, Appolonius of Mainz

persons.name: Leonhardt Kargl
persons.significance: Transcribed and amended Puff von Schrick's work (dated 1499); part of Puff's continuator tradition

persons.name: Friedrich
persons.significance: Laboratory assistant (Laborgehilfe) to the Jankowitz circle; performed hands-on laboratory work for the 1423 gold multiplication experiment. Text states: 'haben wir unsere merung Frydrice czu arbeyten beuolhen' (we assigned our multiplication experiment to Friedrich to work on)

persons.name: Salman Teublein
persons.significance: Jewish alchemist whose secret art was protected by the Landgraves of Leuchtenberg and Counts of Hals. A diploma (later used as binding for Cpg 597) required him not to reveal his art to anyone; if leaving, he must teach his three best procedures under oath. In 1415, negotiated with Duke Frederic of Austria to release a Jewish prisoner from Nuremberg for 600 florins in exchange for revealing his alchemical art. Rec argues Jankowitz's circle were his successors.
persons.voynich_relevance: HIGH - Jewish alchemist in Passau region whose knowledge tradition directly connects to the Alchymey Teuczsch cipher manuscript; demonstrates patronized alchemical secrecy at exact Voynich date

persons.name: Gerhard Eis
persons.significance: Deciphered the Alchymey Teuczsch cipher alphabets (published 1957). Described the manuscript as 'one of the earliest German monuments of alchemical activity and literature'. Concluded secrecy was motivated by 'consideration for fellow humans' — fear that knowledge posed dangers if misused.
sources: Eis, Ostbairische Grenzmarken 1 (1957), pp. 11-16; reprinted in Medizinische Fachprosa (1982), pp. 307-315

persons.name: Rupescissa Glossator (unidentified)
persons.significance: Unidentified figure who wrote a commentary/gloss on Rupescissa's De consideratione quintae essentiae and publicly defended quintessence theory at the University of Padua in 1463 'in einer offenbarlichen versamlung der artzet' (in a public assembly of physicians). Brunschwig's primary authority for quintessence material in the 1512 Large Book — almost all Rupescissa citations go through this intermediary. Represents the key link in the Rupescissa → practical distillation chain.
persons.voynich_relevance: HIGH - Active at Padua during peak Vienna-Padua traffic; transmits Rupescissa's theoretical quintessence into practical distillation tradition; unidentified person at exact right time and place
sources: Brunschwig, Liber de arte distillandi de compositis (1512), lines 5400-5406, 7026-7032, 9281, 10170, 12650, 71850

persons.name: Marsilio Ficino
persons.significance: Renaissance philosopher and physician; translated Plato and Hermes Trismegistus into Latin. His De triplici vita (1489) discusses Aurum potabile and quintessence as life-extending medicine. Brunschwig cites him 7+ times in the 1512 Large Book with specific book and chapter references, names him alongside Arnoldus de Villa Nova as a keeper of the Aurum potabile secret. De triplici vita was widely printed (9+ editions by 1530).
persons.voynich_relevance: MEDIUM - Not in the Voynich's direct temporal-geographic zone but his De triplici vita transmitted quintessence/Aurum potabile knowledge into the German-speaking world via print; Brunschwig's most-cited contemporary authority

persons.name: Jacobus Horcicky de Tepenec
persons.significance: First confirmed owner of the Voynich manuscript (erased signature on fol. 1r, visible under UV). Named Imperial Chemist by Rudolf II (1607). Made fortune distilling Aqua Sinapis (mustard water). Ran herb laboratory at Smichov botanical garden. Cured Rudolf II of grave illness (winter 1608), ennobled October 20, 1608. Lent Rudolf enormous sums; received Melnik estate. Left 50,000 gold coins and Melnik to Jesuits at death. Trained in pharmacy under Martin Schaffner at Krumlov. The Voynich LACKS the Jesuit library mark found on his three other surviving books — critical provenance anomaly.
persons.voynich_relevance: CRITICAL - First confirmed owner; imperial DISTILLER by profession; the convergence between his career (distillation, pharmacy, botanical preparation) and the structural analysis's finding of process-control/distillation encoding is the strongest provenance-structural link in the project

persons.name: Georg Baresch
persons.significance: Earliest confirmed possessor of the Voynich manuscript (by 1637, 'many years' in his library). Described the manuscript as a 'Sphinx' occupying 'useless space.' Initiated correspondence with Athanasius Kircher (c. late 1637, April 1639) seeking decipherment. Identified content as medical, herbal, and chemical. Educated at the Clementinum — the same Jesuit institution where Horcicky was based.
persons.voynich_relevance: HIGH - earliest confirmed possessor; his Clementinum connection to Horcicky suggests a direct institutional transfer path

persons.name: Jan Marek Marci
persons.significance: Inherited the Voynich from Baresch. Chief Physician of Bohemia. Sent the manuscript to Athanasius Kircher in Rome (letter August 19, 1665/1666) with the report that Rudolf II paid 600 ducats for it and that it was believed to be by Roger Bacon (information from Raphael Mnishovsky). 2024 multispectral imaging revealed Marci's handwriting on fol. 1r: three-column substitution cipher attempt producing nonsense.
persons.voynich_relevance: HIGH - transmitted the manuscript to Rome with the key provenance information (600 ducats, Roger Bacon attribution); his decipherment attempt confirmed the manuscript is not a simple substitution

persons.name: Athanasius Kircher
persons.significance: Received the Voynich manuscript from Marci in 1665/1666. Reputed decipherer of Egyptian hieroglyphs (later proven incorrect by Champollion). No evidence he ever responded to Marci about the manuscript or made decipherment progress. The manuscript remained in the Collegio Romano library until Voynich acquired it in 1912.
persons.voynich_relevance: MEDIUM - received the manuscript but apparently could not decipher it; the manuscript entered Jesuit institutional custody through him

persons.name: Rudolf II
persons.significance: Reported to have purchased the Voynich for 600 ducats (via Mnishovsky → Marci). Moved court from Vienna to Prague in 1583. Established legendary Kunstkammer and personal library at Hradschin. Appointed Horcicky as Imperial Chemist. His court attracted Tycho Brahe, Kepler, Kelley, and other scientists and alchemists. The Voynich does NOT appear in the Froeschl inventory of the Kunstkammer (1607-1611).
persons.voynich_relevance: HIGH - probable purchaser of the Voynich; his court was the nexus of Central European alchemy and occult sciences; his personal library (distinct from Kunstkammer) was where the manuscript was likely stored

persons.name: Karl Widemann
persons.significance: Probable seller of the Voynich to Rudolf II. Guzy (2022) identified a book transaction: March 1, 1599, 500 Taler (= 600 Rheinische Gulden) for 'a small barrel with a couple of remarkable/rare books' — the ONLY transaction out of 7,000 journal entries and 126 book transactions matching the 600-ducat amount reported by Mnishovsky. Lived in Leonhard Rauwolf's former house in Augsburg. Worked as secretary to Edward Kelley in Prague (1587-1588). Studied at University of Padua. Dedicated 30+ years to collecting Paracelsus manuscripts. Library catalogue (completed 1629) preserved in Kassel.
persons.voynich_relevance: VERY HIGH - most likely intermediary who sold the Voynich to Rudolf II; connects to BOTH Padua (studied there) and Prague (worked for Kelley); the 600-ducat/gulden match is unique in Rudolf's financial records

persons.name: Leonhard Rauwolf
persons.significance: First European botanist of the post-medieval era to travel in Syria and Mesopotamia (1573-1575). Created multi-volume herbaria: 600+ specimens from France/Italy, 900 from Levant/Mesopotamia. Left Augsburg 1588 (Protestant), retained house. His herbals sold to Rudolf II via Clusius (1593). Died at Waitzen in Hungary (1596); widow died 1597. Widemann lived in his former Augsburg house. If the Widemann-Rauwolf theory is correct, the Voynich may have been in Rauwolf's library — a botanist owning a manuscript with botanical illustrations.
persons.voynich_relevance: HIGH (speculative) - possible prior owner if Widemann sold Rauwolf's books to Rudolf; a botanist owning a botanical cipher manuscript has intrinsic plausibility

persons.name: Raphael Mnishovsky
persons.significance: Source of the claims that Rudolf paid 600 ducats for the Voynich and that Roger Bacon was the author. Reported this to Jan Marek Marci, who transmitted it in the 1665 letter to Kircher. Mnishovsky was himself a cryptographer (author of Constructio seu strues Tritemiana on cipher systems) and studied alchemy for 30+ years. Died 1644, at least 20 years before Marci's letter — the 600-ducat information was at minimum 55 years old when relayed. Some have speculated (without evidence) that Mnishovsky created the Voynich as a cipher demonstration.
persons.voynich_relevance: HIGH - sole source for the 600-ducat purchase claim and the Roger Bacon attribution; his cryptographic expertise is suggestive but not probative

persons.name: Thaddaeus Hagecius
persons.significance: Court polymath under Rudolf II. Hosted John Dee and Edward Kelley in Prague. Served as intermediary for book and manuscript acquisitions. Instrumental in introducing Dee to Rudolf.
persons.voynich_relevance: MEDIUM - key intermediary at Rudolf's court; his role in manuscript acquisitions makes him a potential link in the chain

persons.name: Hugo Blotius
persons.significance: First official Imperial Librarian, appointed by Maximilian II (1575). When Rudolf moved to Prague (1583), Blotius remained in Vienna managing the Hofbibliothek. Facilitated transfer of alchemical and magical texts from the Viennese collection to Rudolf's personal collections in Prague. Also negotiated the Sambucus library acquisition (500 classical manuscripts for 2,500 ducats). Documents an active institutional channel through which Vienna medical/alchemical manuscripts could have reached Prague.
persons.voynich_relevance: MEDIUM - his documented transfers of alchemical books from Vienna to Prague at Rudolf's orders represent a concrete mechanism by which a Vienna manuscript could reach Prague

persons.name: Martin Schaffner
persons.significance: Moravian-born apothecary who trained Jacobus Horcicky de Tepenec in pharmacy at the Cesky Krumlov Jesuit seminary in the 1590s. Taught Horcicky 'practical techniques such as distillation and the preparation of herbal remedies.' Born in Olomouc — the same city where Brunschwig's Kleines Destillierbuch was published in Czech translation in 1559 (translated by Jan Jevicky Cerny, printed by Jan Gunther). No surviving curriculum or formulary from his pharmacy.
persons.voynich_relevance: MEDIUM - trained Horcicky in distillation; born in the city where Brunschwig's Czech translation was published 5 years before his birth; key link between the German distillation tradition and Horcicky's practice

persons.name: Guillaume Rondelet
persons.significance: Montpellier medical professor who trained many of the most important botanists of the 16th century, including Leonhard Rauwolf, Carolus Clusius, Matthias de l'Obel, Felix Platter, and Jacques Dalechamps. His father was an aromatarius (pharmacist/druggist). Reportedly 'introduced alcohol in medicine as an antiseptic and diffused the technique of distillation.' The University of Montpellier had a deep distillation heritage through Arnold of Villanova (c.1240-1311), who sits at the top of our distillation chain (Arnald → Rupescissa → Glossator → Puff → Brunschwig).
persons.voynich_relevance: LOW-MEDIUM - connects Rauwolf and Clusius to the Montpellier distillation tradition that originated with Arnold of Villanova; represents the academic lineage parallel to our Central European distillation chain

persons.name: Carolus Clusius
persons.significance: One of the most important botanists of the 16th century. Trained under Rondelet at Montpellier. Served as prefect of the imperial botanical garden in Vienna under Maximilian II (1573-1577), living with Johann Aicholz. Visited Rauwolf in Augsburg (1565) to examine his herbaria. Corresponded with Rauwolf over many years. Did NOT ultimately broker the sale of Rauwolf's herbaria to Rudolf (Rauwolf sold them directly in 1593 for 310 Reichstaler). Created a pan-European botanical network connecting Montpellier, Vienna, Augsburg, Antwerp, and Leiden.
persons.voynich_relevance: LOW-MEDIUM - connects the Montpellier tradition to Vienna; prefect of imperial botanical garden during the period when distillation knowledge was circulating through the same institutions

persons.name: Johann Aicholz
persons.significance: Professor of medicine at the University of Vienna — the same faculty where Puff von Schrick had been dean eleven times (1435-1473) a century earlier. Clusius's landlord in Vienna during Clusius's time as prefect of the imperial botanical garden (1573-1577). Corresponded with Rauwolf; on May 10, 1581 reported to Camerarius in Nuremberg that he had received plant-care instructions from Rauwolf. Represents institutional continuity between the Puff-era Vienna medical faculty and the Rauwolf-era botanical network.
persons.voynich_relevance: LOW - institutional continuity link between Puff's Vienna and Rauwolf's network; no direct Voynich connection

persons.name: Leonhart Fuchs
persons.significance: One of the three founding fathers of modern botany. His De historia stirpium (1542) contained over 500 plant descriptions with 511 woodcut illustrations — a landmark in botanical illustration. Based at the University of Tubingen where Rauwolf had studied (matriculated 1554). In 1563, Fuchs extensively annotated Rauwolf's three herbarium volumes — one of his final documented scholarly interactions before his death in 1566. The plant genus Fuchsia is named after him.
persons.voynich_relevance: LOW - connected to Rauwolf's botanical training; his illustrated herbal represents the open-publication tradition that contrasts with the Voynich's encoding

persons.name: Johann Bamler
persons.significance: Augsburg printer who produced the FIRST PRINTED EDITION of Puff von Schrick's Büchlein von den ausgebrannten Wässern (1476/1477). This placed the foundational German distillation manual in the same city where Rauwolf would later serve as city physician (1570-1588). Also printed other early German-language books including the Melusine (1474).
persons.voynich_relevance: LOW - establishes that the Puff distillation tradition was physically printed in Augsburg, the city that later connects to the Voynich provenance chain via Rauwolf/Widemann
sources: DeWiki: Büchlein von den ausgebrannten Wässern

persons.name: Johannes von Gmunden
persons.significance: Probably the first dedicated lecturer for mathematical disciplines at a European university. Enrolled at Vienna 1400, BA 1402, MA 1406. Lectured on Aristotle's Physica (1408), Meteorologica (1409, 1411), planetary theory (1406), Euclid (1421), mathematical optics (1414), sexagesimal arithmetic (1412-1417). Dean of Arts Faculty 1413 and 1423. Vice-chancellor. Canon of St. Stephen's Chapter. Bequeathed his entire collection of astronomical/mathematical manuscripts and instruments to the university at death (1442), creating the permanent infrastructure that sustained the 'First Viennese School of Mathematics' (Peuerbach, Regiomontanus). Over 400 manuscripts of his work survive. Active at Vienna throughout the Voynich radiocarbon window (1404-1438).
persons.voynich_relevance: HIGH - dominant Arts faculty figure at Vienna during the exact Voynich radiocarbon window. Taught the natural philosophy (Physica, Meteorologica) that provided the theoretical foundation for distillation science: elements, qualities, transformation, generation and corruption. Every medical student — including those who went on to the medical faculty under Puff's deanship — first studied under Arts faculty masters like Gmunden. His lectures on Physica (1408) and Meteorologica (1409) are the theoretical infrastructure underlying the practical distillation knowledge encoded in the Voynich.
sources: The Renaissance Mathematicus: Vienna and Astronomy

persons.name: Bartholomaeus de Benevento
persons.significance: GHOST FIGURE. Credited as author of the Büchlein von den ausgebrannten Wässern in the 1484 Low German edition (Lübeck, Bartholomäus Gothan): 'meyster Bartholomeus de Benevento (en doctor in d arstedie) dorch leue vnd bede willen erliker erbaren personen / vth velen boken ghesamelt vnde beschreuen' — compiled from many books at the request of honorable people. Modern scholarship notes 'only a smaller portion of the wording comes from Puff himself, while the actual credit belongs to an unknown author' (Müller-Grzenda). If real, he is the actual compiler of the distillation manual that Puff organized and lent institutional authority to. No independent biographical traces found. Benevento is near the Schola Medica Salernitana, suggesting possible southern Italian medical training — a different pipeline from Vienna-Padua.
persons.voynich_relevance: MEDIUM - if the Büchlein's core text was compiled by an Italian physician from 'many books,' it reframes the work as a north-south knowledge transfer product rather than a Vienna faculty original. Parallels the Rupescissa Glossator (P040) as another ghost figure in the distillation chain. Needs identification.
